I'm not a house wife but I am a clean freak and my living space is something of a domestic police state (clean is comforting).

  • Hydrogen peroxide takes stains out of natural fabrics (cotton, linen, silk, etc).
  • Lining the burners with aluminum foil to prevents stuff from getting baked onto the stove.
  • Magic eraser pads take scuffs off enamel fridges, tubs, sinks, etc. They also take off labels, paint, sharpie and glue from jars for reuse. Don't use them on stainless steel though.
  • Most baby wipes can be laundered and reused. Throw them in a lingerie bag and wash with delicates. I use these for wiping glass, electronics and surfaces where I want no streaks.
  • Vinegar for cleaning windows and mirrors (I sometimes stew bay leaves or citrus in mine)
  • Bon Ami for scrubbing the tub
  • Multiple sponges: one for dishes, one for surfaces, one for the bathroom (paper towels to clean the toilet), one for the floor.

Not really a cleaning supply but a good tip for the bachelor. So you're sitting around eating pizza and get a glob of grease on your shirt, or maybe grilling and some greasy meat bits on your shirt and of course your lazy ass throws it in the hamper in a drunken stupor and before you know it, it has gone through the wash and you now have a very clean but unsightly grease stain on your shirt. Never fear, grab some liquid dish detergent, like dawn, or anything that claims to be a grease cutter. Place a few drops on that unsightly grease stain and work it in with a soft brush (old toothbrush works great) or just by rubbing the shirt together on itself. Then throw it back in the wash with a normal load and that grease stain will disappear. If it's really bad you might need to do this a again but I haven't met a stain yet that didn't come out.

When you buy a vacuum, regularly inspect filters and belts and remove hair from the agitator (brush that spins on carpet). It only takes 20 minutes a month max, but you won't have to buy a new vacuum, maybe spend $15 a year on new filters and belts. Plus, your vacuum will always work like new.

Murphy's oil soap is about $2 per bottle, and you have to dilute it, so it lasts quite a while. Use it to polish and dust wood furniture and clean wood cabinets and baseboards. Oh yeah, to avoid streaking, clean anything with a grain in the direction of the grain - even stainless steel. Most stainless appliances made now have a cheap steel veneer that a paper towel can scratch, so just stick to old t shirts or soft rags when cleaning.

Basically, like attracts like, so if you have lime build up, use something acidic (like vinegar). Use something more alkaline when trying to remove soap scum or dirt.
